strategy in the motor rehabilitation of stroke patients.

function by modulating local brain region excitability [11],
[12], [13], the execution of motor behavior relies on dynamic
interactions among multiple brain regions, thereby limiting
its therapeutic efﬁcacy [14], [15]. Dual-Target Brain Region
Stimulation is an emerging neurostimulation strategy that
sequentially stimulates multiple functionally complementary
brain regions, offering advantages in integrating dual-brain
region synergistic effects and optimizing neural signal trans-
mission pathways [16], [17], [18]. Importantly, sequential
dual-target TMS has demonstrated signiﬁcant therapeutic efﬁ-
cacy in conditions such as consciousness disorders, post-stroke
motor function recovery, and cognitive impairments [19], [20],
[21].
In neurostimulation strategies for promoting rehabilitation

of lower limb motor disorders, the supplementary motor
area (SMA) is a commonly used stimulation site for rTMS.
Research indicates that the SMA receives neural inputs from
multiple levels, including primary and secondary somatosen-
sory areas, the parietal association cortex, and projections
from the basal ganglia via the thalamus [22]. These connec-
tions form the basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex-SMA functional
circuit, which is involved in the autonomous generation of
internal movements, automated behaviors, and the planning
and initiation of learned motor sequences [23]. On the other
hand, the SMA sends projection ﬁbers to the corticospinal
tract. As shown in Fig. 1. Through this unique corticospinal
projection, the SMA not only participates in the planning
and initiation stages of movement but also directly intervenes
in the execution process of movement [24]. Notably, recent
studies have shown that the relationship between cognition
and movement is complementary rather than competitive [25].
The results of Yu et al. [26] also conﬁrm that rTMS treatment
of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (L-DLPFC) improves

patients’ balance and postural control abilities and signiﬁcantly
reduces the risk of falls in daily life. Additionally, previous
literature suggests that the L-DLPFC is responsible for plan-
ning, organizing, and regulating motor functions [27], [28]
and may maintain postural control and balance through the
allocation of attentional resources [29]. Another study suggests
that the frontal cortex indirectly inﬂuences basal neural circuits
through projections to the SMA [30]. Therefore, we hypothe-
size that stimulating the L-DLPFC ﬁrst may promote resource
integration within the cognitive-motor network, followed by
stimulation of the SMA to further regulate the immediate reor-
ganization of movement-related networks, thereby enhancing
neural plasticity across multiple brain regions. It should be
noted that “dual-target rTMS” in this study refers to sequential
stimulation of the L-DLPFC and the SMA. However, the
underlying mechanisms of this temporal network regulation
remain poorly understood.
Understanding the potential mechanisms underlying motor

recovery induced by different intervention modalities is cru-
cial for enhancing our understanding of neural mechanisms
and further optimizing motor rehabilitation strategies. Func-
tional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is a neuroimaging
technique used to monitor cortical hemodynamics. Its mea-
surement principle is based on the optical properties of the
medium being studied, so near-infrared light signals are funda-
mentally less susceptible to electromagnetic interference from
TMS pulses and impose no restrictions on the placement of
TMS coils [31], [32]. These characteristics of fNIRS make
it well-suited for use in conjunction with TMS, enabling the
study of the immediate effects of TMS on brain functional
networks.
Traditional static functional connectivity analysis is based

on the assumption that functional interactions between differ-
ent brain regions remain static throughout the scan. However,
brain regions do not interact statically but rather through
dynamic processes [33], [34], [35]. Dynamic functional net-
work connectivity (dFNC) aids in studying dynamic functional
interactions between brain networks and better captures the
dynamic temporal properties of brain functional networks
during TMS stimulation. Therefore, in this study, we aimed
to investigate the effects of single-target and sequential dual-
target stimulation on brain functional networks in stroke
patients (Stroke) and healthy controls (HC) using dFNC anal-
ysis methods with fNIRS. We hypothesize that: (1) there are
signiﬁcant differences in the temporal characteristics of dFNC
between Stroke and HC; (2) changes in the temporal char-
acteristics of dFNC are associated with the severity of lower
limb motor impairments in stroke patients; (3) Compared to
single-target stimulation, sequential dual-target rTMS induces
more pronounced alterations in brain network dynamics.

Center for Rehabilitation Technical Aids. The inclusion cri-

E. Statistical Analysis
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and Levene’s test were used

to assess the variance, normality, and homogeneity of the data
at the group level. A two-sample t-test was employed to detect
group differences in normally distributed data, while the non-
parametric Mann-Whitney U test was used for non-normally
distributed data. Group differences included scores related to
age, gender, MMSE, NIHSS, FMA-LE, and BBS. To exam-
ine the effects on dFNC temporal characteristics, a series
of two-way mixed ANOVAs were conducted with Health
Status (HC vs. Stroke) as a between-subjects factor and Inter-
vention Mode (Resting-state, SMA-rTMS, LDLPFC-rTMS,
Dual-rTMS) as a within-subjects factor. These analyses were
performed separately for the FT of each dFNC state. Post-hoc
comparisons with Bonferroni correction were applied when
signiﬁcant main or interaction effects were found. Finally,
Spearman’s rank correlation analysis was used to explore
the relationship between dFNC temporal characteristics and
clinical variables. Statistical signiﬁcance was set at P < 0.05.
All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version
25.0 software.

by weak connections and low integration, a ﬁnding consistent
with previous studies in patients with schizophrenia, diabetes,
and stroke [50], [55], [56]. This weak connectivity reﬂects
the brain’s baseline connectivity pattern and suggests that
the human brain may tend to maintain this low-efﬁciency
information transmission state to conserve energy [58], [59].
However, we observed a negative correlation between the
FT spent in state 1 during baseline resting conditions in
Stroke and motor function scores. This suggests that the
persistent dominance of this state in pathological contexts
more likely reﬂects impaired network integration capacity.
This ﬁnding aligns with evidence showing that prolonged
dwell time in weak-connectivity states after stroke correlates
with impaired neurological recovery [58], [60]. State 3 exhibits
stronger regional and hemispheric connectivity, consistent with
the characteristics of a “highly integrated state,” but it has
the lowest time proportion (16.32%), potentially reﬂecting
the brain’s efﬁcient information processing capacity within a
limited timeframe.
To more speciﬁcally characterize the connectivity features

of each state, the GE of each state was also calculated.
From the GE perspective, the results of this study align
with ﬁndings from a Parkinson’s disease study indicating
that “higher connectivity states correspond to higher global
efﬁciency” [51]. This suggests that the dynamic layering of
brain networks may follow an “efﬁciency-stability” trade-off
principle, where the high connectivity of State 3 supports
rapid information transmission but comes with higher energy
consumption; the low connectivity of State 1 reduces energy
consumption but may impair cross-regional collaboration. The
differences in this layering across different intervention modes
provide functional-level evidence for understanding brain net-
work reorganization in disease states.
This study also found that, regardless of whether it was

the HC group or the Stroke group, Dual-rTMS signiﬁcantly
increased the FT of State 1 and to some extent reduced the
FT of State 2 and State 3.This phenomenon may suggest
that Dual-rTMS induces a shift in the brain toward a low-
energy state. Additionally, STP results showed that different
stimulation patterns all exhibited signiﬁcant differences from
the resting state to some extent, with Dual-rTMS causing a
signiﬁcant reduction in STP for the transition from State 1 to
State 2 in both the healthy group and the Stroke group.
Research indicates that while intracranial stimulation ini-

tially causes a temporary reduction in the brain network’s
switching capacity and synchrony, this trend gradually stabi-
lizes over time [61]. Intergroup comparisons revealed that the
STP for the transition from State 2 to State 3 was signiﬁcantly
lower in the Stroke group than in the healthy control group.
This indicates impaired ability for the post-stroke brain to
transition from a moderately integrated state to a highly inte-
grated, efﬁcient state. Integrating these ﬁndings, we propose
that this rTMS-induced increase in State 1 FT may repre-
sent a distinct neural mechanism. Speciﬁcally, Dual-rTMS
signiﬁcantly reduced the STP from State 1 to State 2. The
combination of increased State 1 FT and reduced transition
probability suggests that rTMS may actively impose a network
stabilization or reset by disrupting brain network communi-

cation mechanisms. This temporarily suppresses inefﬁcient,
maladaptive ﬂuctuations, enabling the brain to stably maintain
the low-energy State 1, thereby creating an opportunity for
subsequent functional reorganization.
Therefore, this study speculates that sequential dual-target

stimulation may exert a dual regulatory effect on neural
mechanisms: on one hand, by inhibiting the transition from
State 1 to State 2, it reduces inefﬁcient network ﬂuctuations;
on the other hand, the trend toward reduced FT in State
3 may prevent excessive energy consumption and maintain
network homeostasis. This dynamic balance may explain
why sequential dual-target intervention outperforms single-
target stimulation in improving outcomes for lower-limb stroke
patients, as it optimizes the functional coupling efﬁciency
of motor-related brain regions by regulating the temporal
distribution and transition probabilities of network states.

have shown that reduced interhemispheric connectivity is a
core feature of stroke [62], [63]. Siegel et al. [64] previously
proposed that increased modularity is associated with post-
stroke recovery. Our results further suggest that not only the
degree of modularity itself but also the dynamic transition
ability between states may be key indicators of functional
prognosis. Interestingly, while bilateral stimulation primarily
affects State 1 in HC group, it also signiﬁcantly impacts the FT

Stroke brain’s speciﬁc response pattern to neuromodulation.

FT of State 1 in the Stroke group was negatively correlated
with lower limb motor function scores and balance function,
while the FT of State 3 was positively correlated with lower
limb motor function scores and balance function, providing
potential neuroimaging markers for clinical assessment.
The pathological oscillations occurring within the network

may trigger the symptoms induced by the stroke, and stimula-

pathological rhythm [65]. We propose that the interpretation of

disrupt the dynamic rhythms of brain networks, transforming
the current state into a controllable stable state. It is con-
ceivable that establishing new connections from this weakly
connected state may be more feasible, laying the groundwork
for greater network ﬂexibility [66].

stimulation paradigm employed in this study are complex.
A key consideration is the potential inﬂuence of homeo-
static plasticity. Homeostatic plasticity mechanisms ensure
neuronal network excitability remains within physiological

C. Limitations
Our study also has some limitations. First, a potential limita-

tion of this study is the absence of a sham-rTMS control group.
Future experimental designs should include a sham-rTMS
group as a control to better understand the effects of different
stimulation patterns on dynamic brain functional networks.
Second, the selection of sliding window size may inﬂuence
the assessment of dynamic brain connectivity. Future analyses
should be conducted using different window widths to validate
the reliability and reproducibility of the results. Third, the 48-
hour washout period may have been too short to completely
avoid carryover effects between experimental sessions. Fourth,
the localization of stimulation targets (L-DLPFC and SMA)
in this study relied on EEG caps based on the international
10-20 system rather than individualized MRI navigation. This
may introduce some degree of inter-individual variability.
Future studies employing individualized neuro-navigation will
enhance the precision of target localization. Finally, a key
limitation of this study is the absence of resting-state fNIRS
measurements following rTMS intervention. Consequently,
our ﬁndings capture only the immediate online effects of
stimulation, without clarifying whether the observed dynamic
functional network connectivity changes (e.g., increased FT
in state 1) persist as a lasting aftereffect into the post-
stimulation phase. Future studies should incorporate longer
post-intervention monitoring periods to elucidate the temporal
dynamics and potential enduring beneﬁts of sequential dual-
target TMS.

Dual-target
neuromodulation
therapy
is
an
emerging
research direction in neuroscience [69]. A meta-analysis of
22 studies showed that compared to single-target stimula-
tion, sequential dual-target stimulation can achieve higher
efﬁcacy by enhancing neural network plasticity and improv-
ing functional connectivity across cognitive domains [16].
Additionally, high-frequency rTMS (HF-rTMS) applied in a
sequential dual-target stimulation paradigm has been shown to
enhance synaptic efﬁcacy, induce effects similar to long-term
potentiation, and strengthen functional connectivity between
brain regions [70], [71]. Similarly, in this study, HF-rTMS
was sequentially applied to the L-DLPFC and SMA of Stroke
with lower limb motor dysfunction, and it was found that the
connectivity between M1_L, S1_L, and DLPFC_R, SFC_R
varied to different degrees within different dFNC states. This
suggests that the current study protocol may better reshape the
nervous system by optimizing the cross-regional information
integration patterns between the frontal-sensorimotor cortex-
motor cortex loop in patients. The aforementioned mechanisms
and results suggest that rTMS methods based on neural net-
work regulation may promote brain functional remodeling in
Stroke by enhancing synaptic plasticity and repairing damaged
functional connections.
In summary, our study further validates that the therapeu-
tic mechanisms of rTMS can inﬂuence dynamic functional
connectivity between large-scale brain networks. Addition-
ally, dynamic functional connectivity between brain networks
can serve as a predictive indicator of rTMS treatment efﬁ-
cacy. Finally, for Stroke with lower limb motor impairments,
compared to traditional single-target stimulation, sequential
dual-target stimulation may represent an efﬁcient therapeutic
modality to promote brain remodeling.
C. Limitations
Our study also has some limitations. First, a potential limita-
tion of this study is the absence of a sham-rTMS control group.
Future experimental designs should include a sham-rTMS
group as a control to better understand the effects of different
stimulation patterns on dynamic brain functional networks.
Second, the selection of sliding window size may inﬂuence
the assessment of dynamic brain connectivity. Future analyses
should be conducted using different window widths to validate
the reliability and reproducibility of the results. Third, the 48-
hour washout period may have been too short to completely
avoid carryover effects between experimental sessions. Fourth,
the localization of stimulation targets (L-DLPFC and SMA)
in this study relied on EEG caps based on the international
10-20 system rather than individualized MRI navigation. This
may introduce some degree of inter-individual variability.
Future studies employing individualized neuro-navigation will
enhance the precision of target localization. Finally, a key
limitation of this study is the absence of resting-state fNIRS
measurements following rTMS intervention. Consequently,
our ﬁndings capture only the immediate online effects of
stimulation, without clarifying whether the observed dynamic
functional network connectivity changes (e.g., increased FT
in state 1) persist as a lasting aftereffect into the post-
stimulation phase. Future studies should incorporate longer
post-intervention monitoring periods to elucidate the temporal
dynamics and potential enduring beneﬁts of sequential dual-
target TMS.

the writing of this paper.

sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
sections.content:
S

TROKE is a common clinical cerebrovascular disease with
high incidence, mortality, and disability rates. It is mainly

caused by cerebral vascular rupture or embolism, leading to
ischemia and hypoxia in brain tissue, which in turn causes
nerve cell death and seriously affects the health and life of
patients [1], [2]. After a stroke, patients often experience var-
ious neurological sequelae, with hemiplegia being a common
sequela that leads to balance dysfunction and impaired walking
ability. According to reports, nearly 80% of stroke patients
are unable to successfully maintain balance and control their
walking posture [3]. Previous studies have shown that the
neurobiological basis for motor function recovery after stroke
lies in the plasticity of the central nervous system [4], [5].
During this process, the central nervous system reorganizes
its structure and function to reestablish neural connections,
thereby partially compensating for the functional impairments
caused by damage to the lesion area [6], [7]. Therefore,
promoting and restoring neural plasticity is a key intervention
strategy in the motor rehabilitation of stroke patients.

Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a non-invasive

focal brain stimulation technique based on electromagnetic
induction, in which a rapidly changing magnetic ﬁeld induces
small intracranial currents in the brain [8]. The induced
currents cause depolarization of neuronal clusters in the
cortical region directly beneath the stimulation coil, while

also affecting neuronal clusters in adjacent and distant brain
regions, thereby eliciting neurophysiological and behavioral
effects and inducing synaptic-level neuroplasticity changes [9],
[10]. While traditional single-target TMS can improve motor
function by modulating local brain region excitability [11],
[12], [13], the execution of motor behavior relies on dynamic
interactions among multiple brain regions, thereby limiting
its therapeutic efﬁcacy [14], [15]. Dual-Target Brain Region
Stimulation is an emerging neurostimulation strategy that
sequentially stimulates multiple functionally complementary
brain regions, offering advantages in integrating dual-brain
region synergistic effects and optimizing neural signal trans-
mission pathways [16], [17], [18]. Importantly, sequential
dual-target TMS has demonstrated signiﬁcant therapeutic efﬁ-
cacy in conditions such as consciousness disorders, post-stroke
motor function recovery, and cognitive impairments [19], [20],
[21].

In neurostimulation strategies for promoting rehabilitation

of lower limb motor disorders, the supplementary motor
area (SMA) is a commonly used stimulation site for rTMS.
Research indicates that the SMA receives neural inputs from
multiple levels, including primary and secondary somatosen-
sory areas, the parietal association cortex, and projections
from the basal ganglia via the thalamus [22]. These connec-
tions form the basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex-SMA functional
circuit, which is involved in the autonomous generation of
internal movements, automated behaviors, and the planning
and initiation of learned motor sequences [23]. On the other
hand, the SMA sends projection ﬁbers to the corticospinal
tract. As shown in Fig. 1. Through this unique corticospinal
projection, the SMA not only participates in the planning
and initiation stages of movement but also directly intervenes
in the execution process of movement [24]. Notably, recent
studies have shown that the relationship between cognition
and movement is complementary rather than competitive [25].
The results of Yu et al. [26] also conﬁrm that rTMS treatment
of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (L-DLPFC) improves

patients’ balance and postural control abilities and signiﬁcantly
reduces the risk of falls in daily life. Additionally, previous
literature suggests that the L-DLPFC is responsible for plan-
ning, organizing, and regulating motor functions [27], [28]
and may maintain postural control and balance through the
allocation of attentional resources [29]. Another study suggests
that the frontal cortex indirectly inﬂuences basal neural circuits
through projections to the SMA [30]. Therefore, we hypothe-
size that stimulating the L-DLPFC ﬁrst may promote resource
integration within the cognitive-motor network, followed by
stimulation of the SMA to further regulate the immediate reor-
ganization of movement-related networks, thereby enhancing
neural plasticity across multiple brain regions. It should be
noted that “dual-target rTMS” in this study refers to sequential
stimulation of the L-DLPFC and the SMA. However, the
underlying mechanisms of this temporal network regulation
remain poorly understood.

Understanding the potential mechanisms underlying motor

recovery induced by different intervention modalities is cru-
cial for enhancing our understanding of neural mechanisms
and further optimizing motor rehabilitation strategies. Func-
tional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is a neuroimaging
technique used to monitor cortical hemodynamics. Its mea-
surement principle is based on the optical properties of the
medium being studied, so near-infrared light signals are funda-
mentally less susceptible to electromagnetic interference from
TMS pulses and impose no restrictions on the placement of
TMS coils [31], [32]. These characteristics of fNIRS make
it well-suited for use in conjunction with TMS, enabling the
study of the immediate effects of TMS on brain functional
networks.

Traditional static functional connectivity analysis is based

sections.heading: II. MATERIALS AND METHODS
sections.content:
on the assumption that functional interactions between differ-
ent brain regions remain static throughout the scan. However,
brain regions do not interact statically but rather through
dynamic processes [33], [34], [35]. Dynamic functional net-
work connectivity (dFNC) aids in studying dynamic functional
interactions between brain networks and better captures the
dynamic temporal properties of brain functional networks
during TMS stimulation. Therefore, in this study, we aimed
to investigate the effects of single-target and sequential dual-
target stimulation on brain functional networks in stroke
patients (Stroke) and healthy controls (HC) using dFNC anal-
ysis methods with fNIRS. We hypothesize that: (1) there are
signiﬁcant differences in the temporal characteristics of dFNC
between Stroke and HC; (2) changes in the temporal char-
acteristics of dFNC are associated with the severity of lower
limb motor impairments in stroke patients; (3) Compared to
single-target stimulation, sequential dual-target rTMS induces
more pronounced alterations in brain network dynamics.

sections.heading: A. Participants
sections.content:
This study recruited a total of 20 patients with subacute

stroke from the hospital afﬁliated with the National Research
Center for Rehabilitation Technical Aids. The inclusion cri-
teria were as follows: (1) radiological evidence of unilateral

subcortical stroke; (2) age between 20 and 85 years; (3)
the enrollment period was within 7 days and 6 months
after the onset of the disease; (4) presence of mild, mod-
erate, or severe unilateral lower limb motor dysfunction,
as deﬁned by the Fugl-Meyer Assessment for Lower Extrem-
ity (FMA-LE) with the following cutoff scores [36]: severe
(FMA-LE < 19), moderate (FMA-LE 20–28), and mild
(FMA-LE > 29) (5) no contraindications for rTMS mea-
surement; (6) ability to understand and follow instructions.
During the course of this study, three subjects were excluded
due to poor compliance, as they were unable to complete
data collection in accordance with the study requirements.
Additionally, two subjects were excluded after fNIRS data
preprocessing due to excessive motion artifacts resulting in
low signal-to-noise ratios, which did not meet the quality
requirements for fNIRS data analysis. After rigorous data
veriﬁcation, a total of 15 stroke patients were ultimately
included for subsequent analysis. Additionally, 15 healthy
participants matched for age, gender, and educational level,
with no history of mental or neurological disorders, were
recruited as controls. All patients underwent a series of clinical
assessments, including National Institutes of Health Stroke
Scale (NIHSS), Fugl-Meyer Lower Limb Motor Function
Assessment Scale (FMA-LE), Berg Balance Scale (BBS), and
Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). Table I describes
the detailed demographic data and clinical characteristics of
the participants, including age, gender, time since stroke onset,
and cognitive status. According to the Chinese version of the
Dominant Hand Scale [37], all participants were right-handed.
All patients signed informed consent forms and were informed
of potential adverse events prior to the trial. This study (Trial
Registration: ChiCTR2000035984) was approved by Ethics
Committee of Yueyang Integrative Medicine Hospital afﬁliated
to Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine and
strictly adheres to the ethical standards for medical research as
stipulated in the 1975 Helsinki Declaration (revised in 2008).

sections.heading: B. Experimental Design and Procedures
sections.content:
This study is a randomized, prospective, cross-sectional

clinical trial. All participants must complete three experimental
sessions under different intervention conditions, with each
session spaced more than 48 hours apart [38], [39]. The exper-
imental intervention conditions include: (1) SMA single target
stimulation (SMA-rTMS), (2) L-DLPFC single target stimu-
lation (LDLPFC-rTMS), (3) Sequential dual-target rTMS of
the L-DLPFC and SMA (Dual-rTMS). The order of the three
experimental sessions was assigned using a random sequence
generated by MATLAB (The MathWorks, Inc., Natick, MA,
USA) and balanced across participants. Each experimental ses-
sion consisted of two stages: a 6-minute resting-state recording
and a 10-minute transcranial magnetic stimulation interven-
tion. Prior to the experiment, participants were instructed
to rest in a quiet environment for 10-20 minutes to relax
both mentally and physically. Subsequently, fNIRS was used
to simultaneously detect dynamic hemodynamic information
during resting state and rTMS. Additionally, participants were
required to remain awake and avoid voluntary movements and

speech during both the resting state and transcranial magnetic
stimulation.

The TMS used in this study was a magnetic ﬁeld stimulator

with a cone-shaped coil(Yiruide MagTD, Wuhan, China).
For healthy subjects, the resting motor threshold (rMT) was
measured over the right primary motor cortex (M1). The
rMT was deﬁned as the minimum stimulus intensity required
to elicit motor evoked potentials with an amplitude greater
than 50 μV in at least 5 out of 10 stimuli recorded from
the contralateral abductor pollicis brevis muscle. For patients,
if the above method fails to obtain rMT from the affected
side M1, the location of the healthy hemisphere M1 is deﬁned
as the stimulation target, and the healthy hemisphere rMT
is used as the intervention intensity for rTMS. Fig. 2 shows
the intervention parameters for different experimental phases,
as follows: SMA-rTMS: 10 Hz, 100% rMT, 1000 pulses (2
s × 50 trains, 10 s interval); LDLPFC-rTMS: 10 Hz, 80%
rMT, 1000 pulses (5 s × 20 trains, 25 s interval); Dual-rTMS:
5 minutes of LDLPFC-rTMS followed by 5 minutes of SMA-
rTMS, totaling 1000 pulses. Additionally, the stimulation site
for L-DLPFC was located at F3 using the ﬁber cap positioning
from the international 10/20 EEG system [40], and the SMA
stimulation point was deﬁned as the scalp location 3 cm
anterior to the CZ point [41], [42]. All stimulation was admin-
istered by an experienced neurologist who was not involved
in the clinical assessment or data analysis of the participants.

sections.heading: C. fNIRS Measurement and Preprocessing
sections.content:
Brain hemodynamic responses during resting state and TMS

intervention were collected using a multi-channel continuous
wave (740 nm and 850 nm) fNIRS device (NirSmart, Danyang
Huichuang Medical Equipment Co., LTD., Beijing, China)
in a quiet environment. The data sampling frequency was
set to 10 Hz. Following the international 10-20 system [43],
16 detector probes and 18 light source probes were symmetri-
cally arranged on both sides of the prefrontal cortex and motor
cortex, forming a total of 38 signal channels, with a channel
spacing of 30 mm. To achieve precise localization of channel
signals within brain regions, we acquired three-dimensional
coordinates for all probes and key anatomical landmarks
such as the nasal root and preauricular point using a 3D
digitizer. These coordinates were then mapped to the Montreal
Neurological Institute standard space [44]. Subsequently, prob-
abilistic mapping analysis was performed using NIRS-SPM
software [45]. Signals were categorized into 14 regions of
interest based on Brodmann areas: bilateral prefrontal cortex
(PFC), dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), superior frontal
cortex (SFC), presupplementary motor area (PSMA), M1,
primary somatosensory cortex (S1), and occipital cortex (OC).
Additionally, to ensure compatibility with TMS equipment,
a TMS-speciﬁc probe was employed to mitigate limitations
such as shallow TMS penetration depth and susceptibility to
interference.

This study utilized custom routines in MATLAB for fNIRS

data preprocessing, executed via the following procedure.
First, the raw light intensity data were converted into light
density data. Subsequently, the light density data were trans-
formed into oxygenated hemoglobin (HbO2), deoxygenated

motion artifacts and signal spikes [50].

to assess the variance, normality, and homogeneity of the data
at the group level. A two-sample t-test was employed to detect
group differences in normally distributed data, while the non-
parametric Mann-Whitney U test was used for non-normally
distributed data. Group differences included scores related to
age, gender, MMSE, NIHSS, FMA-LE, and BBS. To exam-
ine the effects on dFNC temporal characteristics, a series
of two-way mixed ANOVAs were conducted with Health
Status (HC vs. Stroke) as a between-subjects factor and Inter-
vention Mode (Resting-state, SMA-rTMS, LDLPFC-rTMS,
Dual-rTMS) as a within-subjects factor. These analyses were
performed separately for the FT of each dFNC state. Post-hoc
comparisons with Bonferroni correction were applied when
signiﬁcant main or interaction effects were found. Finally,
Spearman’s rank correlation analysis was used to explore
the relationship between dFNC temporal characteristics and
clinical variables. Statistical signiﬁcance was set at P < 0.05.
All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version
25.0 software.

sections.heading: A. Demographic and Clinical Characteristics
sections.content:
Ultimately, 15 stroke patients and 15 matched healthy con-

trols were included in the ﬁnal data analysis. As summa-rized
in TABLE I, the Stroke group demonstrated signiﬁcantly lower
motor and balance function (as measured by FMA-LE and
BBS scores, p < 0.0001) and higher neurological impairment
(as measured by NIHSS scores, p < 0.0001) compared to the
healthy control group.

sections.content:
The elbow method was used to select the appropriate

number of clusters (K value), as shown in Fig. 4. When K =
3, the rate of change in the total sum of minimum cluster

Additionally, Fig. 5(a) shows the cluster centroids of the

three dFNC matrix states and their percentage occurrence in
the total window, while Fig. 5(b) displays the top 10% of
connection strengths within each state. The results indicate
that state 3 occupies the shortest time proportion in the
total time window (16.32% window proportion), exhibiting
stronger brain functional connectivity patterns and more inter-
hemispheric connections, primarily between M1_L, S1_L, and
DLPFC_R,

brain connectivity strength, with inter-brain region connections
relatively weakened compared to state 3. State 1 occupied the
longest time proportion in the total time window (44.24%
window proportion), characterized by weaker connectivity
within and between all networks, with further weakened
cross-brain region connections, transforming into relatively
stronger intra-brain region connections.

sections.heading: C. Graph-Theoretic Properties and Energy
sections.content:
To delve deeper into the intrinsic characteristics of dif-

ferent states, we characterized them from two dimensions:
network topology and energy metabolism. Fig. 6 illustrates
the differences in graph-theoretic properties among the three
states, where State 3 exhibits the highest GE, followed by
State 2, while State 1 demonstrates signiﬁcantly lower GE (p<
0.0001). Correspondingly, analysis of fNIRS signal power
revealed highly consistent energy consumption patterns (Fig.
7). Speciﬁcally, state 3 is associated with the highest total
signal power, state 2 exhibits intermediate levels, and state
1 demonstrates the lowest total power (p< 0.0001).

sections.heading: D. Time Attributes of Dynamic Functional Network
sections.content:
The ANOVA revealed a signiﬁcant main effect of Inter-

vention Mode on the FT of both State 1 (F(3,112) = 5.35,

p = 0.0018) and State 2 (F(3,112) = 3.27, p = 0.024).
No signiﬁcant main effect of Health Status or interaction
between Health Status and Intervention Mode was found for
any state (all p > 0.05).

Post-hoc analyses, as illustrated in Fig. 8, were performed

to delineate the speciﬁc effects of the interventions. The
results indicated that the FT in State 1 during the Dual-rTMS
intervention was signiﬁcantly higher than in the resting state
for both groups (HC: p = 0.0042; Stroke: p = 0.0185).
Furthermore, the FT of State 1 under SMA-rTMS was also
signiﬁcantly higher than that in the resting state (p = 0.0411).
Notably, the mean FT of State 1 during Dual-rTMS showed
a trend of being higher than that under both single-target
stimulations. In the stroke group, we observed that the FT of
State 2 during the Dual-rTMS intervention was signiﬁcantly
lower than that in the resting state (p = 0.0361). For State 3,
while the main effect of Intervention Mode did not reach strict
statistical signiﬁcance (F(3,112) = 2.54, p = 0.06), the data
trend indicated that the FT of State 3 was relatively lower
during the Dual-rTMS compared to other conditions.

The STP results are shown in Fig. 9. In the HC group,

the STP from State 1 to State 2 was signiﬁcantly lower
under the Dual-rTMS and SMA-rTMS conditions than in
the resting state (Dual-rTMS: p = 0.0009; SMA-rTMS: p =
0.0062). Notably, Dual-rTMS not only signiﬁcantly reduced
the internal state STP of State 2 (p = 0.0372), but also
signiﬁcantly reduced the STP from State 1 to State 2 compared
to LDLPFC-rTMS (p = 0.0324). The Stroke group also
showed that Dual-rTMS and SMA-rTMS signiﬁcantly reduced
the STP from State 1 to State 2 (Dual-rTMS: p = 0.0041;
SMA-rTMS: p = 0.0178). Additionally, in the Stroke group,
both Dual-rTMS and LDLPFC-rTMS signiﬁcantly reduced the
internal STP of State 2 (p =0.0396). Finally, by comparing
group differences using the method of averaging sample values
within each group, the STP from State 2 to State 3 in the
Stroke group was signiﬁcantly lower than that in the HC group
(p = 0.024).

sections.heading: E. Correlation Between dFNC Time Characteristics and
sections.content:
Spearman’s correlation analysis was used to examine the

relationship between dFNC time characteristics and clinical
variables. The results are shown in Fig. 10. In the stroke group,
the FT in State 1 was negatively correlated with Breg and
FMA-LE scores, with the correlation with FMA-LE scores
being statistically signiﬁcant (r = −0.5233, p = 0.0453);

Additionally, the FT in State 3 showed signiﬁcant positive

correlations with both clinical scores (BBS: r = 0.5206, p =
0.0466; FMA-LE: r = 0.5237, p = 0.0451).

sections.heading: IV. DISCUSSION
sections.content:
The human brain is essentially a complex system orga-

nized into a network, and this structure endows it with
high ﬂexibility and enables it to function as a dynamic
system as a whole [55].Therefore, it is necessary to study
the effects of TMS on the brain from a dynamic perspective.
Based on this, we used the dFNC method to investigate

the potential mechanisms underlying brain functional network
remodeling under different rTMS intervention patterns. In this
study, the K-means clustering algorithm was used to iden-
tify three relatively stable and recurrent connection states,
these states exhibit distinct neurological characteristics: State
3 demonstrates the highest GE and total power, representing an
integrated, high-energy-consumption pattern; State 1 exhibits
the lowest GE and power, reﬂecting a low-connectivity, low-
energy-consumption pattern; State 2 presents intermediate
features. Furthermore, rTMS modulated the temporal dynam-
ics of these states: Dual-rTMS signiﬁcantly increased FT of
state 1 while reducing its STP. The study also revealed key
group differences: compared to HC, Stroke exhibited signiﬁ-
cantly reduced STP from state 2 to state 3. Additionally, the

temporal characteristics of dFNC were signiﬁcantly correlated
with patient questionnaire scores. The ﬁndings of this study
provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying the
effects of sequential dual-target TMS.

sections.heading: A. Differences in dFNC Status and Groups
sections.content:
Recent studies have effectively demonstrated the tempo-

ral variability of intrinsic brain networks, indicating that
functional connectivity in the human brain is indeed highly
dynamic, reﬂecting the ﬂexibility of functional coordination
between different brain systems [56], [57]. Consistent with the
results of previous reports, this study identiﬁed three recurrent
dFNC states, with State 1 occupying the largest number
of total time windows. Compared to the other two states,
State 1 exhibits a “sparse connectivity state” characterized

8
IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON NEURAL SYSTEMS AND REHABILITATION ENGINEERING

by weak connections and low integration, a ﬁnding consistent
with previous studies in patients with schizophrenia, diabetes,
and stroke [50], [55], [56]. This weak connectivity reﬂects
the brain’s baseline connectivity pattern and suggests that
the human brain may tend to maintain this low-efﬁciency
information transmission state to conserve energy [58], [59].
However, we observed a negative correlation between the
FT spent in state 1 during baseline resting conditions in
Stroke and motor function scores. This suggests that the
persistent dominance of this state in pathological contexts
more likely reﬂects impaired network integration capacity.
This ﬁnding aligns with evidence showing that prolonged
dwell time in weak-connectivity states after stroke correlates
with impaired neurological recovery [58], [60]. State 3 exhibits
stronger regional and hemispheric connectivity, consistent with
the characteristics of a “highly integrated state,” but it has
the lowest time proportion (16.32%), potentially reﬂecting
the brain’s efﬁcient information processing capacity within a
limited timeframe.

To more speciﬁcally characterize the connectivity features

of each state, the GE of each state was also calculated.
From the GE perspective, the results of this study align
with ﬁndings from a Parkinson’s disease study indicating
that “higher connectivity states correspond to higher global
efﬁciency” [51]. This suggests that the dynamic layering of
brain networks may follow an “efﬁciency-stability” trade-off
principle, where the high connectivity of State 3 supports
rapid information transmission but comes with higher energy
consumption; the low connectivity of State 1 reduces energy
consumption but may impair cross-regional collaboration. The
differences in this layering across different intervention modes
provide functional-level evidence for understanding brain net-
work reorganization in disease states.

This study also found that, regardless of whether it was

the HC group or the Stroke group, Dual-rTMS signiﬁcantly
increased the FT of State 1 and to some extent reduced the
FT of State 2 and State 3.This phenomenon may suggest
that Dual-rTMS induces a shift in the brain toward a low-
energy state. Additionally, STP results showed that different
stimulation patterns all exhibited signiﬁcant differences from
the resting state to some extent, with Dual-rTMS causing a
signiﬁcant reduction in STP for the transition from State 1 to
State 2 in both the healthy group and the Stroke group.

Research indicates that while intracranial stimulation ini-

tially causes a temporary reduction in the brain network’s
switching capacity and synchrony, this trend gradually stabi-
lizes over time [61]. Intergroup comparisons revealed that the
STP for the transition from State 2 to State 3 was signiﬁcantly
lower in the Stroke group than in the healthy control group.
This indicates impaired ability for the post-stroke brain to
transition from a moderately integrated state to a highly inte-
grated, efﬁcient state. Integrating these ﬁndings, we propose
that this rTMS-induced increase in State 1 FT may repre-
sent a distinct neural mechanism. Speciﬁcally, Dual-rTMS
signiﬁcantly reduced the STP from State 1 to State 2. The
combination of increased State 1 FT and reduced transition
probability suggests that rTMS may actively impose a network
stabilization or reset by disrupting brain network communi-

cation mechanisms. This temporarily suppresses inefﬁcient,
maladaptive ﬂuctuations, enabling the brain to stably maintain
the low-energy State 1, thereby creating an opportunity for
subsequent functional reorganization.

Therefore, this study speculates that sequential dual-target

stimulation may exert a dual regulatory effect on neural
mechanisms: on one hand, by inhibiting the transition from
State 1 to State 2, it reduces inefﬁcient network ﬂuctuations;
on the other hand, the trend toward reduced FT in State
3 may prevent excessive energy consumption and maintain
network homeostasis. This dynamic balance may explain
why sequential dual-target intervention outperforms single-
target stimulation in improving outcomes for lower-limb stroke
patients, as it optimizes the functional coupling efﬁciency
of motor-related brain regions by regulating the temporal
distribution and transition probabilities of network states.

sections.heading: B. Network Reorganization Mechanisms in Stroke
sections.content:
This study revealed unique characteristics of functional

network dynamics in Stroke. Compared with healthy controls,
the Stroke group exhibited a reduction in STP from State
2 to State 3, reﬂecting impaired ability to transition to a state
of strong hemispheric connectivity. Similarly, many studies
have shown that reduced interhemispheric connectivity is a
core feature of stroke [62], [63]. Siegel et al. [64] previously
proposed that increased modularity is associated with post-
stroke recovery. Our results further suggest that not only the
degree of modularity itself but also the dynamic transition
ability between states may be key indicators of functional
prognosis. Interestingly, while bilateral stimulation primarily
affects State 1 in HC group, it also signiﬁcantly impacts the FT
of State 2 in the Stroke group, a difference that may reﬂect the
Stroke brain’s speciﬁc response pattern to neuromodulation.
Additionally, our correlation analysis results showed that the
FT of State 1 in the Stroke group was negatively correlated
with lower limb motor function scores and balance function,
while the FT of State 3 was positively correlated with lower
limb motor function scores and balance function, providing
potential neuroimaging markers for clinical assessment.

The pathological oscillations occurring within the network

may trigger the symptoms induced by the stroke, and stimula-
tion of any node within the neural network could disrupt this
pathological rhythm [65]. We propose that the interpretation of
State 1 exhibits dual characteristics: Speciﬁcally, under patho-
logical conditions, the persistent dominance of State 1 indeed
reﬂects a loss of network integration capacity. Conversely,
we suggest that rTMS (particularly dual-target stimulation) can
disrupt the dynamic rhythms of brain networks, transforming
the current state into a controllable stable state. It is con-
ceivable that establishing new connections from this weakly
connected state may be more feasible, laying the groundwork
for greater network ﬂexibility [66].

It is important to note that the neural effects of the temporal

stimulation paradigm employed in this study are complex.
A key consideration is the potential inﬂuence of homeo-
static plasticity. Homeostatic plasticity mechanisms ensure
neuronal network excitability remains within physiological

what would be observed with single-target stimulation alone.

Dual-target
neuromodulation
therapy
is
an
emerging

research direction in neuroscience [69]. A meta-analysis of
22 studies showed that compared to single-target stimula-
tion, sequential dual-target stimulation can achieve higher
efﬁcacy by enhancing neural network plasticity and improv-
ing functional connectivity across cognitive domains [16].
Additionally, high-frequency rTMS (HF-rTMS) applied in a
sequential dual-target stimulation paradigm has been shown to
enhance synaptic efﬁcacy, induce effects similar to long-term
potentiation, and strengthen functional connectivity between
brain regions [70], [71]. Similarly, in this study, HF-rTMS
was sequentially applied to the L-DLPFC and SMA of Stroke
with lower limb motor dysfunction, and it was found that the
connectivity between M1_L, S1_L, and DLPFC_R, SFC_R
varied to different degrees within different dFNC states. This
suggests that the current study protocol may better reshape the
nervous system by optimizing the cross-regional information
integration patterns between the frontal-sensorimotor cortex-
motor cortex loop in patients. The aforementioned mechanisms
and results suggest that rTMS methods based on neural net-
work regulation may promote brain functional remodeling in
Stroke by enhancing synaptic plasticity and repairing damaged
functional connections.

In summary, our study further validates that the therapeu-

tic mechanisms of rTMS can inﬂuence dynamic functional
connectivity between large-scale brain networks. Addition-
ally, dynamic functional connectivity between brain networks
can serve as a predictive indicator of rTMS treatment efﬁ-
cacy. Finally, for Stroke with lower limb motor impairments,
compared to traditional single-target stimulation, sequential
dual-target stimulation may represent an efﬁcient therapeutic
modality to promote brain remodeling.

sections.heading: C. Limitations
sections.content:
Our study also has some limitations. First, a potential limita-

tion of this study is the absence of a sham-rTMS control group.
Future experimental designs should include a sham-rTMS
group as a control to better understand the effects of different
stimulation patterns on dynamic brain functional networks.
Second, the selection of sliding window size may inﬂuence
the assessment of dynamic brain connectivity. Future analyses
should be conducted using different window widths to validate
the reliability and reproducibility of the results. Third, the 48-
hour washout period may have been too short to completely
avoid carryover effects between experimental sessions. Fourth,
the localization of stimulation targets (L-DLPFC and SMA)
in this study relied on EEG caps based on the international
10-20 system rather than individualized MRI navigation. This
may introduce some degree of inter-individual variability.
Future studies employing individualized neuro-navigation will
enhance the precision of target localization. Finally, a key
limitation of this study is the absence of resting-state fNIRS
measurements following rTMS intervention. Consequently,
our ﬁndings capture only the immediate online effects of
stimulation, without clarifying whether the observed dynamic
functional network connectivity changes (e.g., increased FT
in state 1) persist as a lasting aftereffect into the post-
stimulation phase. Future studies should incorporate longer
post-intervention monitoring periods to elucidate the temporal
dynamics and potential enduring beneﬁts of sequential dual-
target TMS.

I. INTRODUCTION
S
TROKE is a common clinical cerebrovascular disease with
high incidence, mortality, and disability rates. It is mainly
caused by cerebral vascular rupture or embolism, leading to
ischemia and hypoxia in brain tissue, which in turn causes
nerve cell death and seriously affects the health and life of
patients [1], [2]. After a stroke, patients often experience var-
ious neurological sequelae, with hemiplegia being a common
sequela that leads to balance dysfunction and impaired walking
ability. According to reports, nearly 80% of stroke patients
are unable to successfully maintain balance and control their
walking posture [3]. Previous studies have shown that the
neurobiological basis for motor function recovery after stroke
lies in the plasticity of the central nervous system [4], [5].
During this process, the central nervous system reorganizes
its structure and function to reestablish neural connections,
thereby partially compensating for the functional impairments
caused by damage to the lesion area [6], [7]. Therefore,
promoting and restoring neural plasticity is a key intervention
strategy in the motor rehabilitation of stroke patients.

sequentially stimulates multiple functionally complementary

In neurostimulation strategies for promoting rehabilitation
of lower limb motor disorders, the supplementary motor
area (SMA) is a commonly used stimulation site for rTMS.
Research indicates that the SMA receives neural inputs from
multiple levels, including primary and secondary somatosen-
sory areas, the parietal association cortex, and projections
from the basal ganglia via the thalamus [22]. These connec-
tions form the basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex-SMA functional
circuit, which is involved in the autonomous generation of
internal movements, automated behaviors, and the planning
and initiation of learned motor sequences [23]. On the other
hand, the SMA sends projection ﬁbers to the corticospinal
tract. As shown in Fig. 1. Through this unique corticospinal
projection, the SMA not only participates in the planning
and initiation stages of movement but also directly intervenes
in the execution process of movement [24]. Notably, recent
studies have shown that the relationship between cognition
and movement is complementary rather than competitive [25].
The results of Yu et al. [26] also conﬁrm that rTMS treatment
of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (L-DLPFC) improves
patients’ balance and postural control abilities and signiﬁcantly
reduces the risk of falls in daily life. Additionally, previous
literature suggests that the L-DLPFC is responsible for plan-

and may maintain postural control and balance through the
allocation of attentional resources [29]. Another study suggests
that the frontal cortex indirectly inﬂuences basal neural circuits
through projections to the SMA [30]. Therefore, we hypothe-
size that stimulating the L-DLPFC ﬁrst may promote resource
integration within the cognitive-motor network, followed by
stimulation of the SMA to further regulate the immediate reor-
ganization of movement-related networks, thereby enhancing
neural plasticity across multiple brain regions. It should be
noted that “dual-target rTMS” in this study refers to sequential
stimulation of the L-DLPFC and the SMA. However, the
underlying mechanisms of this temporal network regulation
remain poorly understood.
Understanding the potential mechanisms underlying motor
recovery induced by different intervention modalities is cru-
cial for enhancing our understanding of neural mechanisms
and further optimizing motor rehabilitation strategies. Func-
tional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is a neuroimaging
technique used to monitor cortical hemodynamics. Its mea-
surement principle is based on the optical properties of the
medium being studied, so near-infrared light signals are funda-
mentally less susceptible to electromagnetic interference from
TMS pulses and impose no restrictions on the placement of
TMS coils [31], [32]. These characteristics of fNIRS make
it well-suited for use in conjunction with TMS, enabling the
study of the immediate effects of TMS on brain functional
networks.
Traditional static functional connectivity analysis is based
on the assumption that functional interactions between differ-
ent brain regions remain static throughout the scan. However,
brain regions do not interact statically but rather through
dynamic processes [33], [34], [35]. Dynamic functional net-
work connectivity (dFNC) aids in studying dynamic functional
interactions between brain networks and better captures the
dynamic temporal properties of brain functional networks
during TMS stimulation. Therefore, in this study, we aimed
to investigate the effects of single-target and sequential dual-
target stimulation on brain functional networks in stroke
patients (Stroke) and healthy controls (HC) using dFNC anal-
ysis methods with fNIRS. We hypothesize that: (1) there are
signiﬁcant differences in the temporal characteristics of dFNC
between Stroke and HC; (2) changes in the temporal char-
acteristics of dFNC are associated with the severity of lower
limb motor impairments in stroke patients; (3) Compared to
single-target stimulation, sequential dual-target rTMS induces
more pronounced alterations in brain network dynamics.
II. MATERIALS AND METHODS
A. Participants
This study recruited a total of 20 patients with subacute
stroke from the hospital afﬁliated with the National Research
Center for Rehabilitation Technical Aids. The inclusion cri-
teria were as follows: (1) radiological evidence of unilateral

subcortical stroke; (2) age between 20 and 85 years; (3)
the enrollment period was within 7 days and 6 months
after the onset of the disease; (4) presence of mild, mod-
erate, or severe unilateral lower limb motor dysfunction,
as deﬁned by the Fugl-Meyer Assessment for Lower Extrem-
ity (FMA-LE) with the following cutoff scores [36]: severe
(FMA-LE < 19), moderate (FMA-LE 20–28), and mild
(FMA-LE > 29) (5) no contraindications for rTMS mea-
surement; (6) ability to understand and follow instructions.
During the course of this study, three subjects were excluded
due to poor compliance, as they were unable to complete
data collection in accordance with the study requirements.
Additionally, two subjects were excluded after fNIRS data
preprocessing due to excessive motion artifacts resulting in
low signal-to-noise ratios, which did not meet the quality
requirements for fNIRS data analysis. After rigorous data
veriﬁcation, a total of 15 stroke patients were ultimately
included for subsequent analysis. Additionally, 15 healthy
participants matched for age, gender, and educational level,
with no history of mental or neurological disorders, were
recruited as controls. All patients underwent a series of clinical
assessments, including National Institutes of Health Stroke
Scale (NIHSS), Fugl-Meyer Lower Limb Motor Function
Assessment Scale (FMA-LE), Berg Balance Scale (BBS), and
Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). Table I describes
the detailed demographic data and clinical characteristics of
the participants, including age, gender, time since stroke onset,
and cognitive status. According to the Chinese version of the
Dominant Hand Scale [37], all participants were right-handed.
All patients signed informed consent forms and were informed
of potential adverse events prior to the trial. This study (Trial
Registration: ChiCTR2000035984) was approved by Ethics
Committee of Yueyang Integrative Medicine Hospital afﬁliated
to Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine and
strictly adheres to the ethical standards for medical research as
stipulated in the 1975 Helsinki Declaration (revised in 2008).
B. Experimental Design and Procedures
This study is a randomized, prospective, cross-sectional
clinical trial. All participants must complete three experimental
sessions under different intervention conditions, with each
session spaced more than 48 hours apart [38], [39]. The exper-
imental intervention conditions include: (1) SMA single target
stimulation (SMA-rTMS), (2) L-DLPFC single target stimu-
lation (LDLPFC-rTMS), (3) Sequential dual-target rTMS of
the L-DLPFC and SMA (Dual-rTMS). The order of the three
experimental sessions was assigned using a random sequence
generated by MATLAB (The MathWorks, Inc., Natick, MA,
USA) and balanced across participants. Each experimental ses-
sion consisted of two stages: a 6-minute resting-state recording
and a 10-minute transcranial magnetic stimulation interven-
tion. Prior to the experiment, participants were instructed
to rest in a quiet environment for 10-20 minutes to relax
both mentally and physically. Subsequently, fNIRS was used
to simultaneously detect dynamic hemodynamic information
during resting state and rTMS. Additionally, participants were
required to remain awake and avoid voluntary movements and
speech during both the resting state and transcranial magnetic
stimulation.
The TMS used in this study was a magnetic ﬁeld stimulator
with a cone-shaped coil(Yiruide MagTD, Wuhan, China).
For healthy subjects, the resting motor threshold (rMT) was
measured over the right primary motor cortex (M1). The
rMT was deﬁned as the minimum stimulus intensity required
to elicit motor evoked potentials with an amplitude greater
than 50 μV in at least 5 out of 10 stimuli recorded from
the contralateral abductor pollicis brevis muscle. For patients,
if the above method fails to obtain rMT from the affected
side M1, the location of the healthy hemisphere M1 is deﬁned
as the stimulation target, and the healthy hemisphere rMT
is used as the intervention intensity for rTMS. Fig. 2 shows
the intervention parameters for different experimental phases,
as follows: SMA-rTMS: 10 Hz, 100% rMT, 1000 pulses (2
s × 50 trains, 10 s interval); LDLPFC-rTMS: 10 Hz, 80%
rMT, 1000 pulses (5 s × 20 trains, 25 s interval); Dual-rTMS:
5 minutes of LDLPFC-rTMS followed by 5 minutes of SMA-
rTMS, totaling 1000 pulses. Additionally, the stimulation site
for L-DLPFC was located at F3 using the ﬁber cap positioning
from the international 10/20 EEG system [40], and the SMA
stimulation point was deﬁned as the scalp location 3 cm
anterior to the CZ point [41], [42]. All stimulation was admin-
istered by an experienced neurologist who was not involved
in the clinical assessment or data analysis of the participants.
C. fNIRS Measurement and Preprocessing

E. Statistical Analysis
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and Levene’s test were used
to assess the variance, normality, and homogeneity of the data
at the group level. A two-sample t-test was employed to detect
group differences in normally distributed data, while the non-
parametric Mann-Whitney U test was used for non-normally
distributed data. Group differences included scores related to
age, gender, MMSE, NIHSS, FMA-LE, and BBS. To exam-
ine the effects on dFNC temporal characteristics, a series
of two-way mixed ANOVAs were conducted with Health
Status (HC vs. Stroke) as a between-subjects factor and Inter-
vention Mode (Resting-state, SMA-rTMS, LDLPFC-rTMS,
Dual-rTMS) as a within-subjects factor. These analyses were
performed separately for the FT of each dFNC state. Post-hoc
comparisons with Bonferroni correction were applied when
signiﬁcant main or interaction effects were found. Finally,
Spearman’s rank correlation analysis was used to explore
the relationship between dFNC temporal characteristics and
clinical variables. Statistical signiﬁcance was set at P < 0.05.
All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version
25.0 software.

A. Differences in dFNC Status and Groups
Recent studies have effectively demonstrated the tempo-
ral variability of intrinsic brain networks, indicating that
functional connectivity in the human brain is indeed highly
dynamic, reﬂecting the ﬂexibility of functional coordination
between different brain systems [56], [57]. Consistent with the
results of previous reports, this study identiﬁed three recurrent
dFNC states, with State 1 occupying the largest number
of total time windows. Compared to the other two states,
State 1 exhibits a “sparse connectivity state” characterized

by weak connections and low integration, a ﬁnding consistent
with previous studies in patients with schizophrenia, diabetes,
and stroke [50], [55], [56]. This weak connectivity reﬂects
the brain’s baseline connectivity pattern and suggests that
the human brain may tend to maintain this low-efﬁciency
information transmission state to conserve energy [58], [59].
However, we observed a negative correlation between the
FT spent in state 1 during baseline resting conditions in
Stroke and motor function scores. This suggests that the
persistent dominance of this state in pathological contexts
more likely reﬂects impaired network integration capacity.
This ﬁnding aligns with evidence showing that prolonged
dwell time in weak-connectivity states after stroke correlates
with impaired neurological recovery [58], [60]. State 3 exhibits
stronger regional and hemispheric connectivity, consistent with
the characteristics of a “highly integrated state,” but it has
the lowest time proportion (16.32%), potentially reﬂecting
the brain’s efﬁcient information processing capacity within a
limited timeframe.
To more speciﬁcally characterize the connectivity features
of each state, the GE of each state was also calculated.
From the GE perspective, the results of this study align
with ﬁndings from a Parkinson’s disease study indicating
that “higher connectivity states correspond to higher global
efﬁciency” [51]. This suggests that the dynamic layering of
brain networks may follow an “efﬁciency-stability” trade-off
principle, where the high connectivity of State 3 supports
rapid information transmission but comes with higher energy
consumption; the low connectivity of State 1 reduces energy
consumption but may impair cross-regional collaboration. The
differences in this layering across different intervention modes
provide functional-level evidence for understanding brain net-
work reorganization in disease states.
This study also found that, regardless of whether it was
the HC group or the Stroke group, Dual-rTMS signiﬁcantly
increased the FT of State 1 and to some extent reduced the
FT of State 2 and State 3.This phenomenon may suggest
that Dual-rTMS induces a shift in the brain toward a low-
energy state. Additionally, STP results showed that different
stimulation patterns all exhibited signiﬁcant differences from
the resting state to some extent, with Dual-rTMS causing a
signiﬁcant reduction in STP for the transition from State 1 to
State 2 in both the healthy group and the Stroke group.
Research indicates that while intracranial stimulation ini-
tially causes a temporary reduction in the brain network’s
switching capacity and synchrony, this trend gradually stabi-
lizes over time [61]. Intergroup comparisons revealed that the
STP for the transition from State 2 to State 3 was signiﬁcantly
lower in the Stroke group than in the healthy control group.
This indicates impaired ability for the post-stroke brain to
transition from a moderately integrated state to a highly inte-
grated, efﬁcient state. Integrating these ﬁndings, we propose
that this rTMS-induced increase in State 1 FT may repre-
sent a distinct neural mechanism. Speciﬁcally, Dual-rTMS
signiﬁcantly reduced the STP from State 1 to State 2. The
combination of increased State 1 FT and reduced transition
probability suggests that rTMS may actively impose a network
stabilization or reset by disrupting brain network communi-
cation mechanisms. This temporarily suppresses inefﬁcient,
maladaptive ﬂuctuations, enabling the brain to stably maintain
the low-energy State 1, thereby creating an opportunity for
subsequent functional reorganization.
Therefore, this study speculates that sequential dual-target
stimulation may exert a dual regulatory effect on neural
mechanisms: on one hand, by inhibiting the transition from
State 1 to State 2, it reduces inefﬁcient network ﬂuctuations;
on the other hand, the trend toward reduced FT in State
3 may prevent excessive energy consumption and maintain
network homeostasis. This dynamic balance may explain
why sequential dual-target intervention outperforms single-
target stimulation in improving outcomes for lower-limb stroke
patients, as it optimizes the functional coupling efﬁciency
of motor-related brain regions by regulating the temporal
distribution and transition probabilities of network states.
B. Network Reorganization Mechanisms in Stroke
Patients and Their Clinical Signiﬁcance
This study revealed unique characteristics of functional
network dynamics in Stroke. Compared with healthy controls,
the Stroke group exhibited a reduction in STP from State
2 to State 3, reﬂecting impaired ability to transition to a state
of strong hemispheric connectivity. Similarly, many studies
have shown that reduced interhemispheric connectivity is a
core feature of stroke [62], [63]. Siegel et al. [64] previously
proposed that increased modularity is associated with post-
stroke recovery. Our results further suggest that not only the
degree of modularity itself but also the dynamic transition
ability between states may be key indicators of functional
prognosis. Interestingly, while bilateral stimulation primarily
affects State 1 in HC group, it also signiﬁcantly impacts the FT
of State 2 in the Stroke group, a difference that may reﬂect the
Stroke brain’s speciﬁc response pattern to neuromodulation.
Additionally, our correlation analysis results showed that the
FT of State 1 in the Stroke group was negatively correlated
with lower limb motor function scores and balance function,
while the FT of State 3 was positively correlated with lower
limb motor function scores and balance function, providing
potential neuroimaging markers for clinical assessment.
The pathological oscillations occurring within the network
may trigger the symptoms induced by the stroke, and stimula-
tion of any node within the neural network could disrupt this
pathological rhythm [65]. We propose that the interpretation of
State 1 exhibits dual characteristics: Speciﬁcally, under patho-
logical conditions, the persistent dominance of State 1 indeed
reﬂects a loss of network integration capacity. Conversely,
we suggest that rTMS (particularly dual-target stimulation) can
disrupt the dynamic rhythms of brain networks, transforming
the current state into a controllable stable state. It is con-
ceivable that establishing new connections from this weakly
connected state may be more feasible, laying the groundwork
for greater network ﬂexibility [66].
It is important to note that the neural effects of the temporal
stimulation paradigm employed in this study are complex.
A key consideration is the potential inﬂuence of homeo-
static plasticity. Homeostatic plasticity mechanisms ensure
neuronal network excitability remains within physiological

connectivity between large-scale brain networks. Addition-

can serve as a predictive indicator of rTMS treatment efﬁ-
cacy. Finally, for Stroke with lower limb motor impairments,
compared to traditional single-target stimulation, sequential
dual-target stimulation may represent an efﬁcient therapeutic
modality to promote brain remodeling.
C. Limitations
Our study also has some limitations. First, a potential limita-
tion of this study is the absence of a sham-rTMS control group.
Future experimental designs should include a sham-rTMS
group as a control to better understand the effects of different
stimulation patterns on dynamic brain functional networks.
Second, the selection of sliding window size may inﬂuence
the assessment of dynamic brain connectivity. Future analyses
should be conducted using different window widths to validate
the reliability and reproducibility of the results. Third, the 48-
hour washout period may have been too short to completely
avoid carryover effects between experimental sessions. Fourth,
the localization of stimulation targets (L-DLPFC and SMA)
in this study relied on EEG caps based on the international
10-20 system rather than individualized MRI navigation. This
may introduce some degree of inter-individual variability.
Future studies employing individualized neuro-navigation will
enhance the precision of target localization. Finally, a key
limitation of this study is the absence of resting-state fNIRS
measurements following rTMS intervention. Consequently,
our ﬁndings capture only the immediate online effects of
stimulation, without clarifying whether the observed dynamic
functional network connectivity changes (e.g., increased FT
in state 1) persist as a lasting aftereffect into the post-
stimulation phase. Future studies should incorporate longer
post-intervention monitoring periods to elucidate the temporal
dynamics and potential enduring beneﬁts of sequential dual-
target TMS.

I. INTRODUCTION
S
TROKE is a common clinical cerebrovascular disease with
high incidence, mortality, and disability rates. It is mainly
caused by cerebral vascular rupture or embolism, leading to
ischemia and hypoxia in brain tissue, which in turn causes
nerve cell death and seriously affects the health and life of
patients [1], [2]. After a stroke, patients often experience var-
ious neurological sequelae, with hemiplegia being a common
sequela that leads to balance dysfunction and impaired walking
ability. According to reports, nearly 80% of stroke patients
are unable to successfully maintain balance and control their
walking posture [3]. Previous studies have shown that the
neurobiological basis for motor function recovery after stroke
lies in the plasticity of the central nervous system [4], [5].
During this process, the central nervous system reorganizes
its structure and function to reestablish neural connections,
thereby partially compensating for the functional impairments
caused by damage to the lesion area [6], [7]. Therefore,
promoting and restoring neural plasticity is a key intervention
strategy in the motor rehabilitation of stroke patients.

In neurostimulation strategies for promoting rehabilitation

Research indicates that the SMA receives neural inputs from
multiple levels, including primary and secondary somatosen-

from the basal ganglia via the thalamus [22]. These connec-

internal movements, automated behaviors, and the planning
and initiation of learned motor sequences [23]. On the other

studies have shown that the relationship between cognition
and movement is complementary rather than competitive [25].
The results of Yu et al. [26] also conﬁrm that rTMS treatment
of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (L-DLPFC) improves
patients’ balance and postural control abilities and signiﬁcantly
reduces the risk of falls in daily life. Additionally, previous
literature suggests that the L-DLPFC is responsible for plan-

noted that “dual-target rTMS” in this study refers to sequential
stimulation of the L-DLPFC and the SMA. However, the
underlying mechanisms of this temporal network regulation
remain poorly understood.
Understanding the potential mechanisms underlying motor
recovery induced by different intervention modalities is cru-
cial for enhancing our understanding of neural mechanisms
and further optimizing motor rehabilitation strategies. Func-
tional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is a neuroimaging
technique used to monitor cortical hemodynamics. Its mea-
surement principle is based on the optical properties of the
medium being studied, so near-infrared light signals are funda-
mentally less susceptible to electromagnetic interference from
TMS pulses and impose no restrictions on the placement of
TMS coils [31], [32]. These characteristics of fNIRS make
it well-suited for use in conjunction with TMS, enabling the
study of the immediate effects of TMS on brain functional
networks.
Traditional static functional connectivity analysis is based
on the assumption that functional interactions between differ-
ent brain regions remain static throughout the scan. However,
brain regions do not interact statically but rather through
dynamic processes [33], [34], [35]. Dynamic functional net-

interactions between brain networks and better captures the
dynamic temporal properties of brain functional networks
during TMS stimulation. Therefore, in this study, we aimed
to investigate the effects of single-target and sequential dual-
target stimulation on brain functional networks in stroke
patients (Stroke) and healthy controls (HC) using dFNC anal-
ysis methods with fNIRS. We hypothesize that: (1) there are
signiﬁcant differences in the temporal characteristics of dFNC
between Stroke and HC; (2) changes in the temporal char-
acteristics of dFNC are associated with the severity of lower
limb motor impairments in stroke patients; (3) Compared to
single-target stimulation, sequential dual-target rTMS induces
more pronounced alterations in brain network dynamics.

B. Experimental Design and Procedures
This study is a randomized, prospective, cross-sectional
clinical trial. All participants must complete three experimental
sessions under different intervention conditions, with each
session spaced more than 48 hours apart [38], [39]. The exper-
imental intervention conditions include: (1) SMA single target
stimulation (SMA-rTMS), (2) L-DLPFC single target stimu-
lation (LDLPFC-rTMS), (3) Sequential dual-target rTMS of
the L-DLPFC and SMA (Dual-rTMS). The order of the three
experimental sessions was assigned using a random sequence
generated by MATLAB (The MathWorks, Inc., Natick, MA,
USA) and balanced across participants. Each experimental ses-
sion consisted of two stages: a 6-minute resting-state recording
and a 10-minute transcranial magnetic stimulation interven-
tion. Prior to the experiment, participants were instructed
to rest in a quiet environment for 10-20 minutes to relax
both mentally and physically. Subsequently, fNIRS was used
to simultaneously detect dynamic hemodynamic information
during resting state and rTMS. Additionally, participants were
required to remain awake and avoid voluntary movements and
speech during both the resting state and transcranial magnetic
stimulation.
The TMS used in this study was a magnetic ﬁeld stimulator
with a cone-shaped coil(Yiruide MagTD, Wuhan, China).
For healthy subjects, the resting motor threshold (rMT) was
measured over the right primary motor cortex (M1). The
rMT was deﬁned as the minimum stimulus intensity required
to elicit motor evoked potentials with an amplitude greater
than 50 μV in at least 5 out of 10 stimuli recorded from
the contralateral abductor pollicis brevis muscle. For patients,
if the above method fails to obtain rMT from the affected
side M1, the location of the healthy hemisphere M1 is deﬁned
as the stimulation target, and the healthy hemisphere rMT
is used as the intervention intensity for rTMS. Fig. 2 shows
the intervention parameters for different experimental phases,
as follows: SMA-rTMS: 10 Hz, 100% rMT, 1000 pulses (2
s × 50 trains, 10 s interval); LDLPFC-rTMS: 10 Hz, 80%
rMT, 1000 pulses (5 s × 20 trains, 25 s interval); Dual-rTMS:
5 minutes of LDLPFC-rTMS followed by 5 minutes of SMA-
rTMS, totaling 1000 pulses. Additionally, the stimulation site
for L-DLPFC was located at F3 using the ﬁber cap positioning
from the international 10/20 EEG system [40], and the SMA
stimulation point was deﬁned as the scalp location 3 cm
anterior to the CZ point [41], [42]. All stimulation was admin-
istered by an experienced neurologist who was not involved
in the clinical assessment or data analysis of the participants.
C. fNIRS Measurement and Preprocessing
Brain hemodynamic responses during resting state and TMS
intervention were collected using a multi-channel continuous
wave (740 nm and 850 nm) fNIRS device (NirSmart, Danyang
Huichuang Medical Equipment Co., LTD., Beijing, China)
in a quiet environment. The data sampling frequency was
set to 10 Hz. Following the international 10-20 system [43],
16 detector probes and 18 light source probes were symmetri-
cally arranged on both sides of the prefrontal cortex and motor
cortex, forming a total of 38 signal channels, with a channel
spacing of 30 mm. To achieve precise localization of channel
signals within brain regions, we acquired three-dimensional
coordinates for all probes and key anatomical landmarks
such as the nasal root and preauricular point using a 3D
digitizer. These coordinates were then mapped to the Montreal
Neurological Institute standard space [44]. Subsequently, prob-
abilistic mapping analysis was performed using NIRS-SPM
software [45]. Signals were categorized into 14 regions of
interest based on Brodmann areas: bilateral prefrontal cortex
(PFC), dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), superior frontal
cortex (SFC), presupplementary motor area (PSMA), M1,
primary somatosensory cortex (S1), and occipital cortex (OC).
Additionally, to ensure compatibility with TMS equipment,
a TMS-speciﬁc probe was employed to mitigate limitations
such as shallow TMS penetration depth and susceptibility to
interference.

data preprocessing, executed via the following procedure.

E. Statistical Analysis
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and Levene’s test were used
to assess the variance, normality, and homogeneity of the data
at the group level. A two-sample t-test was employed to detect
group differences in normally distributed data, while the non-
parametric Mann-Whitney U test was used for non-normally
distributed data. Group differences included scores related to
age, gender, MMSE, NIHSS, FMA-LE, and BBS. To exam-
ine the effects on dFNC temporal characteristics, a series
of two-way mixed ANOVAs were conducted with Health
Status (HC vs. Stroke) as a between-subjects factor and Inter-
vention Mode (Resting-state, SMA-rTMS, LDLPFC-rTMS,
Dual-rTMS) as a within-subjects factor. These analyses were
performed separately for the FT of each dFNC state. Post-hoc
comparisons with Bonferroni correction were applied when
signiﬁcant main or interaction effects were found. Finally,
Spearman’s rank correlation analysis was used to explore
the relationship between dFNC temporal characteristics and
clinical variables. Statistical signiﬁcance was set at P < 0.05.
All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version
25.0 software.
