A. Differences in dFNC Status and Groups
Recent studies have effectively demonstrated the tempo-
ral variability of intrinsic brain networks, indicating that
functional connectivity in the human brain is indeed highly
dynamic, reﬂecting the ﬂexibility of functional coordination
between different brain systems [56], [57]. Consistent with the
results of previous reports, this study identiﬁed three recurrent
dFNC states, with State 1 occupying the largest number
of total time windows. Compared to the other two states,
State 1 exhibits a “sparse connectivity state” characterized

by weak connections and low integration, a ﬁnding consistent
with previous studies in patients with schizophrenia, diabetes,
and stroke [50], [55], [56]. This weak connectivity reﬂects
the brain’s baseline connectivity pattern and suggests that
the human brain may tend to maintain this low-efﬁciency
information transmission state to conserve energy [58], [59].
However, we observed a negative correlation between the
FT spent in state 1 during baseline resting conditions in
Stroke and motor function scores. This suggests that the
persistent dominance of this state in pathological contexts
more likely reﬂects impaired network integration capacity.
This ﬁnding aligns with evidence showing that prolonged
dwell time in weak-connectivity states after stroke correlates
with impaired neurological recovery [58], [60]. State 3 exhibits
stronger regional and hemispheric connectivity, consistent with
the characteristics of a “highly integrated state,” but it has
the lowest time proportion (16.32%), potentially reﬂecting
the brain’s efﬁcient information processing capacity within a
limited timeframe.
To more speciﬁcally characterize the connectivity features
of each state, the GE of each state was also calculated.
From the GE perspective, the results of this study align
with ﬁndings from a Parkinson’s disease study indicating
that “higher connectivity states correspond to higher global
efﬁciency” [51]. This suggests that the dynamic layering of
brain networks may follow an “efﬁciency-stability” trade-off
principle, where the high connectivity of State 3 supports
rapid information transmission but comes with higher energy
consumption; the low connectivity of State 1 reduces energy
consumption but may impair cross-regional collaboration. The
differences in this layering across different intervention modes
provide functional-level evidence for understanding brain net-
work reorganization in disease states.
This study also found that, regardless of whether it was
the HC group or the Stroke group, Dual-rTMS signiﬁcantly
increased the FT of State 1 and to some extent reduced the
FT of State 2 and State 3.This phenomenon may suggest
that Dual-rTMS induces a shift in the brain toward a low-
energy state. Additionally, STP results showed that different
stimulation patterns all exhibited signiﬁcant differences from
the resting state to some extent, with Dual-rTMS causing a
signiﬁcant reduction in STP for the transition from State 1 to
State 2 in both the healthy group and the Stroke group.
Research indicates that while intracranial stimulation ini-
tially causes a temporary reduction in the brain network’s
switching capacity and synchrony, this trend gradually stabi-
lizes over time [61]. Intergroup comparisons revealed that the
STP for the transition from State 2 to State 3 was signiﬁcantly
lower in the Stroke group than in the healthy control group.
This indicates impaired ability for the post-stroke brain to
transition from a moderately integrated state to a highly inte-
grated, efﬁcient state. Integrating these ﬁndings, we propose
that this rTMS-induced increase in State 1 FT may repre-
sent a distinct neural mechanism. Speciﬁcally, Dual-rTMS
signiﬁcantly reduced the STP from State 1 to State 2. The
combination of increased State 1 FT and reduced transition
probability suggests that rTMS may actively impose a network
stabilization or reset by disrupting brain network communi-
cation mechanisms. This temporarily suppresses inefﬁcient,
maladaptive ﬂuctuations, enabling the brain to stably maintain
the low-energy State 1, thereby creating an opportunity for
subsequent functional reorganization.
Therefore, this study speculates that sequential dual-target
stimulation may exert a dual regulatory effect on neural
mechanisms: on one hand, by inhibiting the transition from
State 1 to State 2, it reduces inefﬁcient network ﬂuctuations;
on the other hand, the trend toward reduced FT in State
3 may prevent excessive energy consumption and maintain
network homeostasis. This dynamic balance may explain
why sequential dual-target intervention outperforms single-
target stimulation in improving outcomes for lower-limb stroke
patients, as it optimizes the functional coupling efﬁciency
of motor-related brain regions by regulating the temporal
distribution and transition probabilities of network states.
B. Network Reorganization Mechanisms in Stroke
Patients and Their Clinical Signiﬁcance
This study revealed unique characteristics of functional
network dynamics in Stroke. Compared with healthy controls,
the Stroke group exhibited a reduction in STP from State
2 to State 3, reﬂecting impaired ability to transition to a state
of strong hemispheric connectivity. Similarly, many studies
have shown that reduced interhemispheric connectivity is a
core feature of stroke [62], [63]. Siegel et al. [64] previously
proposed that increased modularity is associated with post-
stroke recovery. Our results further suggest that not only the
degree of modularity itself but also the dynamic transition
ability between states may be key indicators of functional
prognosis. Interestingly, while bilateral stimulation primarily
affects State 1 in HC group, it also signiﬁcantly impacts the FT
of State 2 in the Stroke group, a difference that may reﬂect the
Stroke brain’s speciﬁc response pattern to neuromodulation.
Additionally, our correlation analysis results showed that the
FT of State 1 in the Stroke group was negatively correlated
with lower limb motor function scores and balance function,
while the FT of State 3 was positively correlated with lower
limb motor function scores and balance function, providing
potential neuroimaging markers for clinical assessment.
The pathological oscillations occurring within the network
may trigger the symptoms induced by the stroke, and stimula-
tion of any node within the neural network could disrupt this
pathological rhythm [65]. We propose that the interpretation of
State 1 exhibits dual characteristics: Speciﬁcally, under patho-
logical conditions, the persistent dominance of State 1 indeed
reﬂects a loss of network integration capacity. Conversely,
we suggest that rTMS (particularly dual-target stimulation) can
disrupt the dynamic rhythms of brain networks, transforming
the current state into a controllable stable state. It is con-
ceivable that establishing new connections from this weakly
connected state may be more feasible, laying the groundwork
for greater network ﬂexibility [66].
It is important to note that the neural effects of the temporal
stimulation paradigm employed in this study are complex.
A key consideration is the potential inﬂuence of homeo-
static plasticity. Homeostatic plasticity mechanisms ensure
neuronal network excitability remains within physiological

ally, dynamic functional connectivity between brain networks
can serve as a predictive indicator of rTMS treatment efﬁ-
cacy. Finally, for Stroke with lower limb motor impairments,
compared to traditional single-target stimulation, sequential
dual-target stimulation may represent an efﬁcient therapeutic
modality to promote brain remodeling.
C. Limitations
Our study also has some limitations. First, a potential limita-
tion of this study is the absence of a sham-rTMS control group.
Future experimental designs should include a sham-rTMS
group as a control to better understand the effects of different
stimulation patterns on dynamic brain functional networks.
Second, the selection of sliding window size may inﬂuence
the assessment of dynamic brain connectivity. Future analyses
should be conducted using different window widths to validate
the reliability and reproducibility of the results. Third, the 48-
hour washout period may have been too short to completely
avoid carryover effects between experimental sessions. Fourth,
the localization of stimulation targets (L-DLPFC and SMA)
in this study relied on EEG caps based on the international
10-20 system rather than individualized MRI navigation. This
may introduce some degree of inter-individual variability.
Future studies employing individualized neuro-navigation will
enhance the precision of target localization. Finally, a key
limitation of this study is the absence of resting-state fNIRS
measurements following rTMS intervention. Consequently,
our ﬁndings capture only the immediate online effects of
stimulation, without clarifying whether the observed dynamic
functional network connectivity changes (e.g., increased FT
in state 1) persist as a lasting aftereffect into the post-
stimulation phase. Future studies should incorporate longer
post-intervention monitoring periods to elucidate the temporal
dynamics and potential enduring beneﬁts of sequential dual-
target TMS.
